title: What is known about 1RB0LE_1LB1RC_0RF0RD_1RE0LA_1LA1RE_---0RB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LE_1LB1RC_0RF0RD_1RE0LA_1LA1RE_---0RB.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Open, probably never halting. The tape is always a row of blocks of 1s separated by 00, and the machine treats it as a stack. An exact model of what each sweep does, proved in Lean for all block sizes, shows: from P(n) = E> 00 1^n 01 an odd n leads straight to P((3n+7)/2); an even n starts a recursion that halves the number and pushes blocks on the stack, and ends in one of three ways: a halt (a block pattern (q, r) = (2, 2)), a provable infinite loop ((q, r) = (2, 3)), or a new P(n′), sometimes enormously larger. Lean checks that the run from blank tape survives 80 P-rounds by the kernel (10100 steps) and 650 with native_decide (109,700 steps), with no halt and no loop. For a random start of d digits the chance that the next round halts falls quickly with d, so a halt later on looks unlikely; nothing proves it.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 25,637 cells have been visited and 25,633 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The block model, for every stack and block size
claims.text: With E(S, p, q, r) = 1^S_k 00 … 1^S_1 00 1^p 00 1^q 0 1^r E> 0 (head at the right end, S a stack of blocks) and P(n) = E> 00 1^n 01: q ≥ 4 gives (p+2, q−2, r+1) in 8q+4r−9 steps (and j such rounds at once, by induction); q = 3 gives (p+2, 1, r+1) in 4r+15; q = 2 and r = 1 gives (p+2, 3, 1) in 31; q = 2 and r = 2 halts after 20 steps; q = 2 and r ≥ 3 pushes p+2 and continues with (1, r−2, 1) in 8r; q = 1 merges p, q, r into a block of p+r+4 and pops the stack in 8r+22 (with an empty stack: E([], 0, p+r+4, 1), which reaches P(p+r+4) in 3(p+r+3)+4 more); P(n) goes to E([], 2, n−2, 2) in 5n−6 steps (n ≥ 4). Proved from 12 local rules generated by bbtools.symtm and two crossing lemmas by induction (the head reads one cell beyond each copy, which symtm cannot cross by itself).

claims.title: The run from blank tape follows the model
claims.text: The machine is at P(5) after 51 steps. sweep is one step of the model as a Lean function and sweep_sound proves it for every input; orbit fuel k 5 follows k rounds, and orbit_sound turns any value of it into a statement about the machine.

claims.title: No halt in the first 80 rounds (more than 10<sup>100</sup> steps)
claims.text: The orbit survives 80 P-rounds, evaluated by the kernel; the step count reached is above 10<sup>100</sup>.

claims.title: No halt in the first 650 rounds (more than 10<sup>9,700</sup> steps)
claims.text: The same for 650 P-rounds with native_decide; n then has 16,129 bits. Most rounds grow n by about 3/2, but a deep recursion can multiply its size: round 157 took n from 814 to 7,705 bits.

claims.title: The model against direct simulation
claims.text: The Python transcription of the model reproduces every P-event of the run from blank tape up to 10<sup>10</sup> steps (14 events, n = 5, 11, 20, 67, 104, 277, 419, 632, 2070, 5378, 11434, 24303, 36458, 77479; steps exact), as does the Lean function.

claims.title: The two endings
claims.text: From (p, 2, 3) the machine pushes p+2, merges back to (p+2, 6, 1) and returns to (p+6, 2, 3) in 2 sweeps: once (q, r) = (2, 3) occurs it never halts (a block-level translated cycler). (q, r) = (2, 2) halts after 21 steps. Nothing else ends a round.

claims.title: Halting gets rarer as n grows
claims.text: Fraction of random starts P(n) whose next round halts or loops forever, by number of digits of n: 6 digits: 4.4% halt, 1.5% loop; 8 digits: 2.7%, 0.8%; 10 digits: 2.0%, 0.6%; 12 digits: 1.0%, 0.35%; 15 digits: 0.55%, 0.3%; 20 digits: 0.25%, 0.03% (4,000 random starts each). The fraction drops quickly with the size of n, and n has thousands of digits after 650 rounds, so a halt after that looks very unlikely. No probability model behind this is worked out yet.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It halts if and only if some round of the orbit from P(5) reaches (q, r) = (2, 2); it provably never halts if one first reaches (2, 3).

explainer.lede: Probably never, but nobody can prove it yet. This machine keeps its tape as a stack of blocks of 1s and runs a small recursive program on their sizes. From P(n) an odd n simply becomes (3n+7)/2; an even n sets off a recursion that halves it, and the recursion can end in a halt, in an endless loop, or in a new, larger n. Lean proves the program exactly, and checks that for 650 rounds (more than 10<sup>9,700</sup> steps) it never halts.

facts.text: Every sweep of the block program is proved in Lean for all block sizes, with exact step counts.
No halt in 650 rounds (Lean, native_decide); 80 rounds and 10<sup>100</sup> steps by the kernel alone.
The chance that a round halts falls fast with the size of n.

sections.heading: A stack of blocks and a small recursive program
html: At every moment the tape is a row of blocks of 1s separated by double zeros. The head goes back and forth over the last three blocks, called p, q and r, and the blocks further left wait, like the entries of a stack.

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 110" role="img" aria-label="the tape as a stack of blocks" style="width:100%;max-width:560px;height:auto;font:12px var(--mono);"><rect x="10" y="30" width="70" height="26" fill="var(--line)" fill-opacity=".25" stroke="var(--line)"/><text x="45" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">1^S1</text><text x="92" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">00</text><rect x="104" y="30" width="60" height="26" fill="var(--line)" fill-opacity=".25" stroke="var(--line)"/><text x="134" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">1^S2</text><text x="176" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">00</text><rect x="188" y="30" width="90" height="26" fill="var(--accent)" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="var(--accent)"/><text x="233" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">1^p</text><text x="290" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">00</text><rect x="302" y="30" width="140" height="26" fill="var(--accent)" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="var(--accent)"/><text x="372" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">1^q</text><text x="450" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">0</text><rect x="458" y="30" width="60" height="26" fill="var(--accent)" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="var(--accent)"/><text x="488" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">1^r</text><rect x="520" y="30" width="26" height="26" fill="var(--head)" fill-opacity=".25" stroke="var(--head)"/><text x="533" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">E</text><text x="95" y="80" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">the stack</text><text x="380" y="80" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">the three working blocks</text><text x="280" y="102" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">each sweep moves two 1s from q to p and one to r</text></svg>
Each sweep of the head moves two 1s from q to p and adds one to r, until q is nearly empty. What happens then depends on the last few 1s:

whenwhat happens
q ≥ 3two 1s go from q to p, one more 1 on r
q = 1merge: p, q and r become one block of p+r+4; the top of the stack becomes the new p (if the stack is empty: a new P round)
q = 2, r = 1q becomes 3, keep going
q = 2, r ≥ 3push: p+2 goes on the stack, and the work restarts on a block of r−2
q = 2, r = 3, again and againan endless loop: never halts
q = 2, r = 2halt

Every so often all blocks merge into one and the tape is P(n) = E> 00 1^n 01 with the head at the left end. From blank tape this happens with n = 5, 11, 20, 67, 104, 277, 419, 632, 2070, …. For odd n the round is simple: the next n is (3n+7)/2. For even n the block q runs down to 2 with r = n/2, the program pushes a block and starts over on a block about half as long, and the recursion can go many levels deep before everything merges back.

sections.heading: Only if the recursion hits one exact small case
html: The machine halts only when it meets q = 2 with r = 2, and it is caught in an endless loop if it meets q = 2 with r = 3 first. Both need the halving recursion to come down to a very small block, which takes a long run of lucky halvings.

Measured on random starting values, the chance that a round ends in a halt drops quickly as n gets longer: 6 digits: 4.4% halt, 1.5% loop; 8 digits: 2.7%, 0.8%; 10 digits: 2.0%, 0.6%; 12 digits: 1.0%, 0.35%; 15 digits: 0.55%, 0.3%; 20 digits: 0.25%, 0.03% (4,000 random starts each).

Lean has followed the run from blank tape for 650 rounds; n then has 16,129 binary digits and the step count has more than 9,700 decimal digits. It never met either ending. A proof that it never halts would need to understand this recursion for all n, which nobody has done.

sections.heading: Proved in Lean: the program, and 10<sup>9,700</sup> steps
html:
• Kernel: 12 local rules (generated by py/rules.py), two crossing loops by induction, and from them every case of the block program for all stacks and block sizes, with exact step counts.
  • Kernel: blank tape reaches P(5) in 51 steps; 80 rounds without a halt, more than 10100 steps.
  • native_decide: 650 rounds without a halt, more than 109,700 steps.
  • Measured: how often a round halts, by size of n.
  • Open: whether the run ever halts.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.046). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.473).
After 109 steps the tape spans 25,637 cells (24 left of the start, 18,466 right), with a density of 1s of 1.0.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

family: block stack machine: P(n) → P((3n+7)/2) for odd n, a halving recursion with a stack for even n
summary: An exact block model: the tape is blocks of 1s separated by 00, handled like a stack; P(n) = E> 00 1<sup>n</sup> 01 goes to P((3n+7)/2) for odd n and into a halving recursion for even n, which can halt, run away forever, or return to a new P; model proved in Lean, no halt for 650 rounds (10<sup>9,700</sup> steps, native_decide).
